sentences.t:
Ðā ic æt þearfe [gefrægn] þēodcyninges
andlongne eorl ellen cȳðan,
cræft ond cēnðu, swā him gecynde wæs.
sentences.l: Then I [heard] at the need the people-king’s upright earl show courage, skill and boldness, as was natural to him.
sentences.i: Then, as I have heard, in that hour of need the king’s own man, standing upright, showed his courage, his skill and his daring, as was natural to him.
sentences.n: The pattern is ‘ic … gefrægn’ + accusative + infinitive, ‘I heard (the earl) show’; ‘cȳðan’ is the infinitive of ‘cȳðan’, ‘make known, show’, and ‘ellen’, ‘cræft’ and ‘cēnðu’ (‘courage’, ‘skill’, ‘boldness’) are its three objects. The verb is Kemble’s addition, which is why Klaeber prints ‘[gefrægn]’ in square brackets: the manuscript line has none, and ‘ic gefrægn’, ‘I have heard tell’, is the poet’s usual way of citing the tradition. ‘þēodcyninges’ is a genitive and depends on ‘eorl’, ‘the people-king’s earl’, that is, Beowulf’s man, Wīglāf, who is named at 2745. ‘andlongne’ is a guess: ‘andlang’ means ‘along, continuous’ and also ‘upright, erect’, and ‘standing upright’ suits a man who is on his feet beside his fallen lord, but ‘throughout’ or ‘unbroken’ are also possible. ‘swā him gecynde wæs’ is ‘as was natural to him’ (‘gecynde’ ‘inborn’, with the dative ‘him’).

sentences.t:
Ne hēdde hē þæs heafolan, ac sīo hand gebarn
mōdiges mannes, þǣr hē his mǣges healp,
þæt hē þone nīðgæst nioðor hwēne slōh,
secg on searwum, þæt ðæt sweord gedēaf
fāh ond fǣted, þæt ðæt fȳr ongon
sweðrian syððan.
sentences.l: He did not heed the head, but the hand burned of the brave man, where he helped his kinsman, so that he struck the hostile spirit somewhat lower, the man in armour, so that the sword sank in, shining and plated, so that the fire began to lessen afterwards.
sentences.i: He paid no heed to the head, but the brave man’s hand was scorched as he helped his kinsman, so that he struck the hateful creature somewhat lower down, armoured as he was, and the bright plated sword sank in, and the fire began to die down after that.
sentences.n: A chain of clauses hangs on one another: ‘þǣr hē his mǣges healp’ (‘where he helped his kinsman’), then three with ‘þæt’, each giving a result: ‘þæt hē … slōh’ (‘so that he struck’), ‘þæt ðæt sweord gedēaf’ (‘so that the sword sank in’; ‘þæt’ is the conjunction and ‘ðæt’ the article; ‘gedēaf’ is the past of ‘gedūfan’, ‘dive, sink’) and ‘þæt ðæt fȳr ongon sweðrian’ (‘so that the fire began to lessen’). ‘ne hēdde … þæs heafolan’ is ‘did not heed the head’, with a genitive object after ‘hēdan’; the contrast, I take it, is with Beowulf’s own blow, which was aimed at the dragon’s head and broke his sword on it, so Wīglāf strikes lower. That reading is an inference from the verse just before this part. ‘sīo hand gebarn’ is ‘the hand burned’ (‘gebarn’ is the past of ‘gebeornan’, intransitive). ‘mǣges’ has italic ‘es’ because the manuscript has ‘mægenes’, ‘of strength’; Kemble’s ‘mǣges’, ‘kinsman’s’ (read here as the object of ‘healp’, which can take the genitive), is followed. ‘nīðgæst’ is ‘hostile spirit’ (‘nīð’ ‘malice’ + ‘gǣst’ ‘spirit’), the dragon; ‘hwēne’ ‘a little’; ‘secg on searwum’ ‘the man in armour’ is Wīglāf, in apposition to ‘hē’. Editors differ over these ‘ðæt’s: Sievers and Holthausen delete the one at 2700, and Grundtvig, Sievers and Sedgefield read ‘þā ðæt’ at 2701; some also read ‘þā’ for ‘þæt’ before ‘hē’ at 2699. ‘fāh ond fǣted’ I take as ‘gleaming and plated’, of the sword, but ‘fāh’ also means ‘hostile’ and the sense is not certain. ‘sweðrian’ is ‘die down, subside’, said of the fire; the dragon’s fire shrinks once he is hit in the body.

sentences.l: Then still the king himself ruled his wits, drew the slaughter-knife, bitter and battle-sharp, which he bore on the byrnie;
sentences.i: Then the king himself, still in command of his wits, drew the deadly knife, keen and sharp for battle, that he wore on his mail-shirt;
sentences.n: ‘gewēold … gewitte’ is ‘controlled his wits’ (‘gewealdan’ with a dative object), and ‘þā gēn’ is ‘even then’, ‘as yet’: the point is that Beowulf is badly hurt and still thinks clearly. ‘gebrǣd’ is the past of ‘gebregdan’, ‘draw’, and takes ‘wæll-seaxe’ in the dative-instrumental. Klaeber prints the hyphen: ‘wæl’ is ‘slaughter, the slain’ and a ‘seax’ is the single-edged knife the Saxons are named from, a short weapon worn at the belt; E. Sc., Holthausen and Sedgefield read the bare ‘-seax’ in place of ‘-seaxe’. ‘biter ond beaduscearp’ is ‘bitter and battle-sharp’ (‘beadu’ ‘battle’ + ‘scearp’ ‘sharp’), and the relative ‘þæt’ is the neuter ‘seax’; ‘hē on byrnan wæg’ is ‘he carried on the mail-shirt’, ‘wæg’ the past of ‘wegan’, ‘carry, wear’. The knife is a last weapon: his sword Nægling burst at 2680, after he struck the dragon’s head.

sentences.t: forwrāt Wedra helm wyrm on middan.
sentences.l: The helm of the Weders cut the worm through in the middle.
sentences.i: and the protector of the Weders cut the dragon through at the middle.
sentences.n: ‘forwrāt’ is the past of ‘forwrītan’, ‘cut through, slash apart’ (the verb ‘write’ began as ‘score, incise’), and ‘wyrm’ is its object; ‘on middan’ is ‘in the middle’. ‘Wedra helm’ is ‘the helm of the Weders’, the poem’s phrase for Beowulf, ‘helm’ being the ‘helmet’ that covers and so the protector, and the Weders being the Geats; the same phrase named Hrēðel at 2462, so it is a title for the Geat king rather than a name. The stroke is the knife’s: after Wīglāf’s blow has weakened the fire, the king himself finishes the beast.

sentences.l: They felled the foe — courage drove out life —, and they had then both destroyed him, the kin-athelings;
sentences.i: They brought the enemy down — courage drove the life out of him —, and the two of them together had destroyed him, noble kinsmen both;
sentences.n: ‘gefyldan’ is the past plural of ‘gefyllan’, ‘fell, make fall’, and ‘fēond’ is its object, so the subject is the two men named only by the pronoun ‘hī’ in the next clause (E. Sc., Thorpe, Sievers and Sedgefield read the singular ‘gefylde’, ‘he felled’, as if one man struck). The dashes enclose ‘ferh ellen wræc’, ‘courage drove out life’: ‘ferh’ (‘life, spirit’) and ‘ellen’ are both neuter, so their forms do not say which is subject and which object; I take ‘ellen’ as the subject and ‘ferh’ as the object, and ‘wræc’ is the past of ‘wrecan’, ‘drive’; I take the life driven out to be the dragon’s, but that is a guess, since the words would fit the heroes’ own life being driven on by courage. Kemble wrote ‘ferh-ellen’ as one word, ‘life-courage’; Klaeber prints two words; the apparatus also records Kluge’s ‘ealne’ for ‘ellen’ (‘all’) and Aantekeningen’s ‘ellor’ (‘elsewhere’). ‘ābroten hæfdon’ is a pluperfect, ‘had destroyed’ (‘ābroten’ is the participle of ‘ābrēotan’, ‘destroy, kill’), and ‘bēgen’ is ‘both’. ‘sibæðelingas’ is ‘kin-athelings’: ‘sib’ is ‘kinship’, and ‘æðeling’ ‘prince, nobleman’, so ‘noble kinsmen’, in apposition to ‘hī’; the poem called Beowulf Wīglāf’s ‘mǣg’, kinsman, at 2675, with no detail given.

sentences.t:
swylc sceolde secg wesan,
þegn æt ðearfe!
sentences.l: such should a man be, a thane at need!
sentences.i: That is how a man ought to be, a thane in time of need!
sentences.n: ‘swylc’ (‘such’) looks back to what the two men have just done, and ‘sceolde’ is the preterite of ‘sculan’ used for what ought to be: ‘such a man should be’, as a general judgement rather than a report of one occasion. ‘secg’ and ‘þegn’ are two words for the man, and ‘æt ðearfe’ is ‘at need’ (dative of ‘þearf’), as at 2694; the poet steps out of the narrative to give the lesson, and the exclamation mark is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
Þæt ðām þēodne wæs
sīðas[t] sigehwīla sylfes dǣdum,
worlde geweorces.
sentences.l: That was for the prince, by his own deeds, the last of victory-times, of work in the world.
sentences.i: That was the last of the prince’s hours of victory, won by his own deeds, the end of his work in the world.
sentences.n: ‘Þæt’ is the subject of ‘wæs’, ‘that was’, looking back to the killing of the dragon, and ‘ðām þēodne’ is a dative, ‘for the prince’. ‘sīðast sigehwīla’ is ‘the last of victory-times’ (‘sigehwīla’ a genitive plural of ‘sigehwīl’, ‘victory-time’; ‘sīðast’ the superlative ‘last’, used as a noun): Klaeber has changed the manuscript at two places, adding the ‘t’ in square brackets and the italic ‘a’; the manuscript reads ‘siðas sige hwile’, and the editors give a long list of other readings (Kemble ‘sīðes sigehwīl’, Grein ‘sīðast sigehwīla’, Grundtvig and Bugge ‘sīðast sigehwīle’, Trautmann and four other editors ‘sīðast sigehwīl’), none of which changes the general sense. ‘sylfes dǣdum’ is ‘by his own deeds’ (dative plural, instrumental). ‘worlde geweorces’ is the hard phrase: I read ‘worlde’ as ‘in the world’ and ‘geweorces’ as a genitive going with ‘sigehwīla’, ‘of work in the world’, meaning the achievements of his life; that is a guess, and nothing in the apparatus helps. This is the last triumph the poem gives Beowulf.

sentences.l: Then the wound began, which for him the earth-dragon had earlier wrought, to burn and to swell;
sentences.i: Then the wound that the earth-dragon had dealt him began to burn and to swell;
sentences.n: ‘sīo wund ongon … swelan ond swellan’ is ‘the wound began to burn and swell’: ‘ongon’ takes the two infinitives, ‘swelan’ (‘burn, be inflamed’) and ‘swellan’ (‘swell’), a pair that sound almost alike. ‘þē him se eorðdraca ǣr geworhte’ is a relative clause put between ‘ongon’ and its two infinitives: ‘which the earth-dragon had made for him earlier’ (‘þē’ ‘which’, ‘him’ a dative, ‘geworhte’ the past of ‘gewyrcan’, ‘work, make’). ‘eorðdraca’ is ‘earth-dragon’ (‘eorðe’ ‘earth’ + ‘draca’ ‘dragon’), the beast that lives in the ground; the wound is the bite in his neck from the last part. The venom goes on working after the fight is over.

sentences.t:
hē þæt sōna onfand,
þæt him on brēostum bealonīð(e) wēoll
attor on innan.
sentences.l: he found that at once, that in his breast, with bale-malice, poison welled within.
sentences.i: he soon found that venom was welling up within his breast with baleful malice.
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ in ‘hē þæt sōna onfand’ looks ahead to the second ‘þæt’, ‘that’, which opens the clause that follows, with ‘onfand’ the past of ‘onfindan’, ‘find out, perceive’. ‘him on brēostum’ is ‘in his breast’ (‘him’ a dative of possession; ‘brēostum’ a plural used where we use a singular). ‘bealonīð’ is ‘bale-malice’ (house rendering from Fitt XXV): ‘bealu’ is ‘evil, harm’ and ‘nīð’ ‘malice, hatred’. The ending in parentheses is a letter Klaeber restores where the scorched manuscript is lost: the two Thorkelin transcripts give ‘mð’ and ‘niði’, and Schubert, Sievers and four more read ‘-nīðe’, which I take as a dative, ‘with baleful malice’; the sense is the same either way. ‘attor’ is the subject of ‘wēoll’ (‘welled’) and means ‘poison, venom’, and ‘on innan’ ‘within’.

sentences.l: Then the atheling went, so that he by the wall, wise-thinking, sat on a seat;
sentences.i: Then the prince went, and sat down by the wall, thoughtful, on a ledge;
sentences.n: ‘gīong’ is a spelling of ‘gēong’, the past of ‘gangan’, ‘go’, and ‘þæt’ gives the result: ‘went so that he sat’, that is, went across and sat down. ‘bī wealle’ is ‘by the wall’ (dative). ‘wīshycgende’ is the present participle of a compound of ‘wīs’ (‘wise’) and ‘hycgan’ (‘think’), ‘wise-thinking’, which I read as ‘thoughtful, in his right mind’; Klaeber gives no gloss here that I can quote, so the shade is a guess. ‘sesse’ is the dative of ‘sess’, ‘seat’ (the word is related to ‘session’), and here must be a ledge or bench of stone in the barrow. ‘æðeling’ is again Beowulf.

sentences.t:
seah on enta geweorc,
hū ðā stānbogan stapulum fæste
ēce eorðreced innan healde.
sentences.l: he looked on the work of giants, how the stone arches, fast on pillars, held the eternal earth-hall within.
sentences.i: and looked on the work of giants, on how the stone arches, firm upon their pillars, held up the everlasting earth-hall inside.
sentences.n: ‘seah on’ is ‘looked on’, with ‘enta geweorc’ (‘the work of giants’) as its object, and the clause that follows is an indirect question introduced by ‘hū’, ‘how’, so ‘healde’ is a subjunctive. Its subject ‘stānbogan’ is plural and ‘healde’ looks singular; Holthausen reads the plural ‘hēoldon’, but Klaeber keeps the manuscript form, so the number clash is left standing. ‘stapulum’ is a dative plural, ‘on pillars’ (‘stapol’ ‘pillar, post’), with ‘fæste’ ‘firmly’. ‘eorðreced’ is ‘earth-hall’, ‘reced’ being ‘hall, building’ (a different word from ‘sele’ in ‘eorðsele’ at 2410, but the same barrow); Holthausen reads ‘ēcne’ for ‘ēce’, but ‘ēce’, ‘eternal’, can be an accusative neuter as it stands. ‘enta geweorc’ is a standing phrase for old stone-work, often Roman, that the English of the time could not account for and ascribed to giants; here it names the barrow’s vault, as ‘enta ǣrgeweorc’ does at 1679, of the sword-hilt.

sentences.t:
Hyne þā mid handa heorodrēorigne,
þēoden mǣrne þegn ungemete till,
winedryhten his wætere gelafede
hilde sædne ond his hel(m) onspēon.
sentences.l: Him then with hands — the sword-gory one, the famous prince — the thane, exceedingly good, laved with water, his friend-lord, battle-sated, and unfastened his helm.
sentences.i: Then the thane, so very good, with his hands bathed his lord with water, his famous prince, bloody from the sword and weary of battle, and loosed his helmet.
sentences.n: The sentence is a long one in which the order hides the subject: ‘þegn ungemete till’ (‘the thane exceedingly good’) is the nominative, and ‘Hyne’, ‘þēoden mǣrne’ and ‘winedryhten’ are three accusative words naming the one man, Beowulf, with ‘heorodrēorigne’ (‘sword-gory’, ‘heoru’ ‘sword’ + ‘drēorig’ ‘gory’) and ‘hilde sædne’ (‘sated with battle’; ‘hilde’ is a genitive or dative form of ‘hild’, ‘battle’, and ‘sæd’ can take the genitive) added. ‘gelafede’ is ‘laved, bathed’ and takes ‘wætere’ in the dative; ‘onspēon’ is the past of ‘onspanan’, ‘unfasten’, with ‘his hel(m)’ as its object. ‘winedryhten’ is ‘friend-lord’ (‘wine’ ‘friend’ + ‘dryhten’ ‘lord’). The letter in parentheses is Klaeber’s restoration: the two Thorkelin transcripts read ‘helo’ and ‘heb’, and E. Sc., following Grimm, reads ‘helm’. Zupitza, who collated the manuscript, noted a mark like an angle above the ‘t’ of ‘till’ that he could not interpret, and Klaeber prints the word plain. ‘till’ is ‘good, apt’, and the thane is Wīglāf.

sentences.t:
Bīowulf maþelode — hē ofer benne spræc,
wunde wælblēate;
sentences.l: Beowulf spoke in speech-words — he spoke over his wound, the slaughter-wretched wound;
sentences.i: Beowulf spoke in formal words — he spoke over his wound, the deadly wound;
sentences.n: ‘Bīowulf maþelode’ is the house formula, ‘spoke in speech-words’ (‘spoke in formal words’ in the idiomatic version), and what follows between the dash and the semicolon says how: ‘hē ofer benne spræc’ is ‘he spoke over the wound’, with ‘benne’ in the dative and ‘ofer’ here perhaps meaning ‘with the wound upon him’ or ‘about’; the preposition is not clear, so I have kept ‘over’. ‘wunde wælblēate’ is ‘the wound, slaughter-wretched’, a second dative in apposition. ‘wælblēate’ is a guess: ‘wæl’ is ‘slaughter’ and ‘blēat’ ‘wretched’, so ‘slaughter-wretched’, but Grein, Scheinert and Holthausen read ‘-blāte’, from ‘blāt’, ‘pale, livid’, which would give ‘deadly-pale’. The speech that follows is Beowulf’s last long one.

sentences.l: he knew clearly that he had lived through his day-times, earth’s joy;
sentences.i: he knew full well that he had lived out his days and the joys of earth;
sentences.n: ‘wisse’ is the past of ‘witan’, ‘know’, and ‘gearwe’ is the adverb ‘clearly, fully’. The ‘þæt’ clause has ‘gedrogen hæfde’, a pluperfect built on the participle of ‘gedrēogan’, ‘pass through, endure’, with ‘dæghwīla’ (‘day-times’, an accusative plural, which has the same form as the genitive plural) as its object. ‘eorðan wynn(e)’ is ‘earth’s joy’, in apposition, a way of saying the pleasure of living on earth. I take ‘wynne’ as accusative; the parenthesis is Klaeber’s restoration where the scorched edge is lost, and the final ‘e’ is the reading of Thorkelin and of Grundtvig’s translation.

sentences.t:
ðā wæs eall sceacen
dōgorgerīmes, dēað ungemete nēah —:
sentences.l: then was all gone of his day-count, death immeasurably near —:
sentences.i: then the whole number of his days had run out, and death stood very near —
sentences.n: ‘eall sceacen dōgorgerīmes’ is ‘all gone of the day-count’: ‘sceacen’ is the past participle of ‘scacan’, ‘depart’, and ‘dōgorgerīmes’, a genitive singular of ‘dōgorgerīm’ (‘dōgor’ ‘day’ + ‘gerīm’ ‘number’), says what has gone, the whole of his reckoned days. ‘dēað ungemete nēah’ is a clause with no verb, ‘death immeasurably near’ (the same words, ‘ungemete nēah’, were said of fate at 2420). The dash and colon open the speech that follows, which runs to the end of the part.

sentences.t:
‘Nū ic suna mīnum syllan wolde
gūðgewǣdu, þǣr mē gifeðe swā
ǣnig yrfeweard æfter wurde
līce gelenge.
sentences.l: ‘Now I would give to my son the war-garments, if it were so granted me that any heir after me should become, of my body belonging.
sentences.i: ‘Now I would give my battle-gear to my son, if it were granted me that any heir of my own body should come after me.
sentences.n: ‘ic … syllan wolde’ is ‘I would give’, and ‘þǣr’ opens a condition, ‘if’, with a subjunctive in it: ‘þǣr mē gifeðe swā … wurde’ is ‘if it were so granted to me that … should come’ (‘gifeðe’ is an adjective, ‘granted’, and ‘wurde’ a past subjunctive of ‘weorþan’, ‘become’). ‘ǣnig yrfeweard’ is ‘any heir’ (‘yrfe’ ‘inheritance’ + ‘weard’ ‘guardian’), and ‘līce gelenge’ is ‘belonging to the body’, that is, of his own flesh; the phrase is a dative with an adjective, and ‘gelenge’ means ‘dependent on, belonging to’. ‘gūðgewǣdu’ is ‘war-garments’, his armour. ‘mīnum’ is the dative ‘to my’, with ‘suna’ the dative of ‘sunu’. The opening quotation mark is Klaeber’s.

sentences.t:
Ic ðās lēode hēold
fīftig wintra;
sentences.l: I held these people fifty winters;
sentences.i: I ruled this people for fifty years;
sentences.n: ‘Ic ðās lēode hēold’ is ‘I held these people’, ‘lēode’ the accusative plural, and ‘fīftig wintra’ is ‘fifty of winters’, the genitive plural of ‘winter’ used for the time: the English reckoned years by winters. The poem gave the same count at 2208–09, of his rule; the semicolon ends a short boast that is the first of a list.

sentences.t:
næs sē folccyning,
ymbesittendra ǣnig ðāra,
þē mec gūðwinum grētan dorste,
egesan ðeôn.
sentences.l: there was not that folk-king, any of those around-sitters, who dared to approach me with war-friends, to threaten with terror.
sentences.i: there was no king of the neighbouring peoples, not one of them all, who dared to meet me with his warriors or to bring terror on me.
sentences.n: ‘næs’ is ‘ne wæs’, ‘was not’, and the subject is ‘sē folccyning’ (‘that people-king’), with the apposition ‘ymbesittendra ǣnig ðāra’ (‘any of the around-sitters of those’; ‘ymbesittendra’ is the genitive plural of ‘ymbesittend’, ‘one who sits around’, a neighbour, the same house rendering as in the prologue and at 1826–27); Thorpe, Trautmann and Holthausen read ‘ymb-’ for ‘ymbe-’. The relative clause is ‘þē mec gūðwinum grētan dorste’, ‘who dared to approach me with war-friends’: ‘grētan’ means ‘touch, approach’ and so, in the hostile sense, ‘assail’, and ‘gūðwinum’ is a dative plural, ‘war-friends’, comrades in arms. ‘egesan ðeôn’ is ‘to threaten with terror’ (the infinitive ‘ðeôn’, with its circumflex for a contracted vowel, I read as the verb ‘press, urge’, and ‘egesan’ a dative of means); the second infinitive is a guess in its exact sense, but the phrase matches ‘egesan þȳwað’ at 1827, ‘press with terror’.

sentences.t:
Ic on earde bād
mǣlgesceafta, hēold mīn tela,
sentences.l: I awaited at home the time-fates, held my own well,
sentences.i: I waited at home for what fate allotted me, and kept well what was mine,
sentences.n: ‘bād’ is the past of ‘bīdan’, ‘wait for’, which here takes a genitive, ‘mǣlgesceafta’ (a genitive plural, ‘of the time-fates’); ‘on earde’ is ‘at home, in my own land’ (dative). ‘mǣlgesceaft’ is a word that occurs only here, and I give it as a guess: ‘mǣl’ is ‘a fixed time, a mark’ and ‘gesceaft’ ‘decree, destiny’, so ‘the destinies set for their times’. ‘hēold mīn tela’ is ‘held my own well’, ‘mīn’ a neuter accusative used as a noun, ‘what is mine’, and ‘tela’ the adverb ‘well, rightly’. The king’s boast is of keeping to his own and not making wars.

sentences.t:
ne sōhte searonīðas, nē mē swōr fela
āða on unriht.
sentences.l: did not seek cunning-hatreds, nor swore many oaths for myself wrongly.
sentences.i: I did not look for crafty quarrels, nor did I swear many false oaths.
sentences.n: The subject ‘ic’ carries over from the last unit, with two negative verbs: ‘ne sōhte’ (‘did not seek’) and ‘nē … swōr’ (‘nor swore’), ‘swōr’ the past of ‘swerian’. ‘searonīðas’ is ‘cunning-hatreds’ (‘searo’ ‘device, craft’ + ‘nīð’ ‘hatred, strife’), the house rendering: plots and treacherous feuds. ‘mē’ is a dative of interest, ‘for myself’, and ‘fela āða’ is ‘many oaths’ (‘fela’ takes the genitive plural). ‘on unriht’ is ‘in wrong’, that is, wrongly, falsely. The mark Zupitza saw over the ‘n’ of ‘unriht’ is the sign that he described at 2721; Klaeber prints the word plain.

sentences.t:
Ic ðæs ealles mæg
feorhbennum sēoc gefēan habban;
sentences.l: I of all this may, sick with life-wounds, have joy;
sentences.i: In all this, sick as I am with my mortal wounds, I can still take joy;
sentences.n: ‘ðæs ealles’ is a genitive, ‘for all this’, giving the ground of the joy; ‘gefēan habban’ is ‘have joy’ (‘gefēa’ a weak noun, ‘joy’), and ‘mæg’ ‘can, may’. ‘feorhbennum sēoc’ is ‘sick with life-wounds’, a dative plural of ‘feorhbenn’ (‘feorh’ ‘life’ + ‘benn’ ‘wound’), a wound that touches the life, mortal wounds; the compound is new to the house list. The plural is odd for one man’s wound, and I take it as a general plural, wounds in the body.

sentences.t:
forðām mē wītan ne ðearf Waldend fīra
morðọrbealo māga, þonne mīn sceaceð
līf of līce.
sentences.l: therefore the Wielder of men need not charge me with murder-bale of kinsmen, when my life departs from the body.
sentences.i: and so the Ruler of men need not charge me with the murder of kinsmen when my life departs from my body.
sentences.n: ‘forðām’ is ‘therefore’, and the sentence is built on ‘mē wītan ne ðearf Waldend’: ‘ne ðearf’ is ‘need not’ (the preterite-present ‘þurfan’), ‘wītan’ the infinitive of ‘wītan’, ‘reproach, charge with’ (a different verb from ‘witan’, ‘know’), taking a dative of the person (‘mē’) and the thing as accusative, here ‘morðọrbealo’. ‘Waldend fīra’ is ‘Wielder of men’, a title of God as at 1661, ‘ylda Waldend’. ‘morðọrbealo māga’ is ‘murder-bale of kinsmen’, the same words as at 1079 (‘morþọrbealo māga’, said of Hildeburh), where the point was the killing of kin; it is the worst of sins in the poem’s world, and Beowulf’s claim is that he has none on him. The dot under the ‘ọ’ of ‘morðọrbealo’ is Klaeber’s sign that the vowel does not count in the metre, so the word is scanned as if it were absent; it is the first and only one in this part, and it does not change the sense. ‘þonne’ is ‘when’, and ‘mīn sceaceð līf of līce’ ‘my life departs from the body’, with ‘sceaceð’ the third singular of ‘scacan’, ‘depart’.

sentences.t:
Nū ðū lungre geong
hord scēawian under hārne stān,
Wīglāf lēofa, nū se wyrm ligeð,
swefeð sāre wund, since berēafod.
sentences.l: Now go you quickly to look at the hoard under the hoar stone, dear Wīglāf, now that the worm lies, sleeps sorely wounded, of treasure bereft.
sentences.i: Now go quickly, dear Wīglāf, and look upon the hoard beneath the grey stone, now that the dragon lies sleeping, sorely wounded and robbed of his treasure.
sentences.n: ‘geong’ is an imperative, ‘go’, a variant of ‘gong’ and Kemble’s ‘gang’ (it is not the adjective ‘geong’, ‘young’), and ‘hord scēawian’ is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to look at the hoard’; ‘under hārne stān’ is ‘under the hoar stone’ (the phrase of 2553), ‘hār’ meaning grey with age. ‘Wīglāf lēofa’ is a vocative, ‘dear Wīglāf’, with the weak form ‘lēofa’. ‘nū se wyrm ligeð’ begins a ‘nū’ clause, ‘now that the dragon lies’, with one more verb, ‘swefeð’ (‘sleeps’), and two participles, ‘wund’ and ‘berēafod’ (‘robbed of’, with ‘since’ ‘treasure’ in the dative). ‘swefeð’ may be ‘sleeps’ meant as a gentle word for dead, since 2705 says the dragon was cut through, or it may mean that he is still alive and unconscious; the poem does not say which. ‘nū’ stands at 2743 and again at 2745, which gives the command its urgency.

sentences.t:
Bīo nū on ofoste, þæt ic ǣrwelan,
goldǣht ongite, gearo scēawige
swegle searogimmas, þæt ic ðȳ sēft mæge
æfter māððumwelan mīn ālǣtan
līf ond lēodscipe, þone ic longe hēold.’
sentences.l: Be now in haste, that I the ancient-wealth, the gold-possession, may perceive, ready may behold the bright cunning-gems, that I the more softly may after the treasure-wealth leave my life and people-realm, which I long held.’
sentences.i: Be quick now, that I may see the ancient wealth, the hoard of gold, and eagerly look on the bright jewels of cunning make, so that, after that wealth of treasure, I may the more gently give up my life and the kingdom I held so long.’
sentences.n: ‘Bīo’ is an imperative of ‘wesan’ (‘be’), and ‘on ofoste’ ‘in haste’. Two ‘þæt’ clauses follow with subjunctives of purpose: ‘þæt ic … ongite … scēawige’ (‘that I may perceive … behold’) and ‘þæt ic … ālǣtan’ (‘that I may give up’, an infinitive after ‘mæge’). ‘ǣrwelan’ is ‘ancient-wealth’ (‘ǣr’ ‘early, former’ + ‘wela’ ‘wealth’) and ‘goldǣht’ ‘gold-possession’ (‘āht’ ‘property’), both accusatives for the hoard. ‘gearo’ is ‘ready’ (Ettmüller and Aantekeningen read the adverb ‘gearwe’, ‘clearly’). ‘swegle searogimmas’ is hard: ‘searogimmas’ is ‘cunning-gems’ (‘searo’ ‘skilled work’ + ‘gimm’ ‘gem’), and I read ‘swegle’ as an adjective ‘bright’ agreeing with it, a guess from the noun ‘swegl’ ‘sky’; Thorpe reads ‘sigel’ (‘jewel’), Holthausen ‘siglu’ and Rieger ‘sigle’, ‘ornaments’. ‘ðȳ sēft’ is ‘the more softly’ (‘ðȳ’ the instrumental ‘by that’ before a comparative), and ‘æfter māððumwelan’ is ‘after the treasure-wealth’, that is, once he has seen it. ‘lēodscipe’ is ‘people-realm’, the nation, and the relative ‘þone’ points back to it. The closing quotation mark ends Beowulf’s speech; the poem puts his last wish into this request to see the gold.
